clips.text: Respiratory rate counts breaths per minute. A commonly taught resting adult range is twelve to twenty, but age, activity, and clinical circumstances matter. Monitors may estimate breathing from changes in electrical impedance between chest electrodes. Such estimates can contain artifact or miss important problems. A displayed number is not the same as observing breathing depth, effort, pattern, and the person being monitored.

clips.text: Pulse oximetry estimates the percentage of hemoglobin binding sites occupied by oxygen in pulsating arterial blood. The device compares absorption of red and infrared light. It does not directly measure total oxygen content, ventilation, or carbon dioxide. Think of saturation as the fraction of seats occupied on oxygen-carrying buses, not the number of buses available. That is why hemoglobin concentration and blood flow also matter for oxygen delivery.

clips.text: Many healthy people at sea level have readings from ninety-five to one hundred percent. One hundred percent is not automatically abnormal, and a pulse-oximeter reading alone does not establish oxygen toxicity. Motion, poor perfusion, nail products, dyshemoglobins, and device limitations can affect results. Accuracy can also differ across skin pigmentation. Carbon monoxide exposure can produce misleading readings on ordinary pulse oximeters. Interpret the measurement in context, not as a stand-alone assurance.

clips.text: Capnography displays carbon dioxide in exhaled gas over time. End-tidal carbon dioxide is the value near the end of exhalation. A common reference range in a healthy resting adult is thirty-five to forty-five millimeters of mercury, but the value depends on ventilation, perfusion, metabolism, and equipment. The waveform changes as exhaled gas moves from conducting-airway gas toward alveolar gas. It is not interchangeable with a direct arterial carbon dioxide measurement.

clips.text: Match each tool to the question it helps answer. Respiratory rate describes frequency. Pulse oximetry estimates arterial oxygen saturation. Capnography reflects exhaled carbon dioxide and ventilation-related information. The E C G records electrical activity of the heart. None of these alone proves adequate perfusion or gives a complete assessment. This lesson teaches what the signals mean, not how to prescribe oxygen, perform resuscitation, or choose a treatment.
